source.why_this_one: D-005: everything committed under evidence/ must come from the open corpus. This is openly licensed and quotable in full.
source.PAGE_LABELS_ARE_PROPOSED: The passages were retrieved as HTML, which has no PDF pagination. The page_label values below are ASSIGNED BY SECTION ORDER, not read from a PDF. They exercise the label/index split correctly, but they are NOT verifiable against a printed page. The label-vs-index mechanism itself was already proven in 2C against a real PDF with a real /PageLabels tree; what this fixture is for is faithfulness, not pagination. A genuine end-to-end page check needs the OpenStax PDF.

SCOPE_LIMITS.read_this_before_quoting_any_number: Two limits bound everything measured against this file. Neither is a defect in the fixture; both change what its numbers mean, and both are easy to forget once a number has been written down once.
SCOPE_LIMITS.1_this_is_a_ceiling_not_a_typical_case: One OpenStax chapter: clean, digital-native, professionally edited, English. Aakar's real input is scanned Indian textbooks — photographed or flatbed-scanned pages, mixed scripts, marginalia, tighter typesetting, and prose that was not written to be machine-read. Faithfulness measured here is close to the best this system will ever do. Nothing about it predicts the failure rate on the actual corpus; it establishes that the failures we DO see on a clean chapter are real, since the input cannot be blamed for them.
SCOPE_LIMITS.2_c06_tests_the_display_path_not_ocr_noi: c06 carries `source: "ocr"` and is otherwise clean, verbatim text. It exercises the SECOND AXIS — that an OCR-derived citation reaches the student marked differently from a digital one (D-044, D-047) — and it exercises nothing about whether real OCR errors cause citation failures. Those are different questions. A chunk with genuine artefacts (transposed characters, split or merged words, a dropped diacritic, a column read across the gutter) would test whether a garbled chunk still gets cited as though it were sound, and whether the lexical support check silently scores a misread word as unsupported. FUTURE WORK: add one chunk of real Tesseract output over a real scanned page, alongside the digital text of the same page, and measure the difference.
SCOPE_LIMITS.what_would_close_these: A second golden set built from an actual scanned textbook page, OCR'd by the real pipeline, with labels verified by hand against the printed page. That closes the pagination gap above and both limits here at once, and it is the fixture that would let these numbers speak about the product rather than about the method.

chunks.text: The eye itself is a hollow sphere composed of three layers of tissue. The outermost layer is the fibrous tunic, which includes the white sclera and clear cornea.
The transparent cornea covers the anterior part of the eye. It allows light to enter, and along with the lens, focuses light onto the retina.

The middle layer of the eye is the vascular tunic, which is mostly composed of the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The choroid is a layer of highly vascularized connective tissue that provides a blood supply to the eyeball.

Overlaying the ciliary body, and visible in the anterior eye, is the iris—the colored part of the eye. The iris is a smooth muscle that opens or closes the pupil, which is the hole at the center of the eye that allows light to enter.
The innermost layer of the eye is the neural tunic, or retina, which contains the nervous tissue responsible for photoreception.

The anterior cavity is the space between the cornea and lens, including the iris and ciliary body. It is filled with a watery fluid called the aqueous humor. The posterior cavity is the space behind the lens that extends to the posterior side of the interior eyeball, where the retina is located. The posterior cavity is filled with a more viscous fluid called the vitreous humor.
The photoreceptors (rods and cones) change their membrane potential when stimulated by light energy.
At the fovea, the retina lacks the supporting cells and blood vessels, and only contains photoreceptors. Therefore, visual acuity, or the sharpness of vision, is greatest at the fovea.

There are two types of photoreceptors—rods and cones—which differ in the shape of their outer segment. The rod-shaped outer segments of the rod photoreceptor contain a stack of membrane-bound discs that contain the photosensitive pigment rhodopsin. The cone-shaped outer segments of the cone photoreceptor contain their photosensitive pigments in infoldings of the cell membrane.
The axons of RGCs, which lie at the innermost layer of the retina, collect at the optic disc and leave the eye as the optic nerve.
